h1: Handling beer consumer complaints and what quality teams check
title: Handling Beer Consumer Complaints | Craft Beer School
desc: How drinks companies handle beer consumer complaints, the common complaint types and what quality teams check, from batch codes to retained samples.
teaser: A complaint about a flat beer from one bar in Pune might be a bad keg, a dirty line or a batch problem. The quality team's job is to find out which.
standfirst: Every beer company gets complaints. Most are about storage and serving rather than brewing. A few point to a real batch problem. Customer service, sales and quality teams need a shared process to tell them apart quickly.
sections:
A complaint is free quality data from the market. It can reveal a cold chain problem in one region, a faulty packaging run or a batch that slipped past release checks. It can also reveal nothing more than a warm bottle or a dirty glass. Treating every complaint seriously and investigating in a consistent way, is how a company learns which is which.

Handled badly, a complaint becomes a social media post. Handled well, it can turn an unhappy drinker into a loyal one and give the brewery a warning it would not otherwise get.

• Taste or smell: stale, cardboard, sour, skunky, metallic or simply "not like usual".
  • Flat or overly fizzy beer, including gushing when opened.
  • Appearance: haze in a normally clear beer, sediment or floating particles.
  • Foreign matter: glass, insects or other objects in the pack.
  • Pack defects: low fill, leaking crowns, dented cans or damaged labels.
  • Effects after drinking: complaints that the drinker felt unwell, which need careful, respectful handling and escalation.

Stale and cardboard notes usually point to oxidation, often made worse by heat in storage. Our guide to oxidised beer explains how it happens.
Step one: capture the right details

The first contact sets up the whole investigation. Customer service should record:

  • Brand, pack type and size.
  • The batch code and best before date printed on the pack, ideally with a photo.
  • Where and when it was bought and how it was stored.
  • What the drinker noticed, in their own words.
  • Whether the product is still available to collect.

Without a batch code, the quality team can only guess. Training front line staff to ask for it politely is the single most useful improvement many companies can make.
Step two: what quality teams check

With a batch code, quality can trace the pack back to its production records. The usual checks are:

  • Batch release records: lab results for alcohol, carbonation, oxygen, clarity and micro, plus the sensory sign-off. See how a beer batch is released.
  • Retained samples: breweries keep library samples from each batch. Tasting and testing them shows whether the beer was right when it left.
  • Other complaints: are there more from the same batch, line or region? One complaint is an incident. Several from one batch is a pattern.
  • Packaging records: line stoppages, fill level checks and seam or crown checks from that run.
  • The returned product itself, if it can be collected.

Most investigations end in one of three findings. The batch was fine and the problem was storage, serving or handling in the market. The batch had a real but limited issue, such as one packaging run with low fills. Or there is a wider problem that needs action across the market.

For the first two, the response is a clear, courteous reply and often a replacement. For the third, the company may need to hold stock and, in serious cases, recall. Our guide to the beer recall plan covers that decision. Foreign matter and illness complaints should always go to senior quality staff quickly.

Many complaints in India trace back to heat. Beer that sat in a hot warehouse, a truck or a shop with no cooling will taste stale earlier than its date suggests. Green and clear bottles left in sunlight develop a skunky aroma quickly. Draught complaints in bars often come from dirty lines, wrong gas pressure or kegs stored warm.

Quality teams that track complaints by region and month often see a summer peak. That data is useful for supply chain and sales teams, not only for the brewery.

Every investigation should end with a recorded root cause and, where possible, a corrective action. Monthly reviews that show complaint rates per million packs, by type and region, turn individual incidents into trends. When customer service, sales and quality all understand the process, the company gets faster answers and fewer repeat complaints.

Share the findings back with the people who took the call. A customer service agent who learns that most stale complaints come from one hot depot will ask sharper questions next time. The sales team can raise storage with that distributor directly.
faqs: What is the most important detail to collect in a beer complaint?
The batch code and best before date on the pack. They let the quality team trace the beer to its production records and retained samples.
Why do many beer complaints come from storage rather than brewing?
Heat and light damage beer after it leaves the brewery. Warm warehouses, trucks and shops speed up staling. Sunlight causes a skunky aroma in clear or green glass.
A sample kept from each production batch so the brewery can test and taste it later if a complaint or question comes up.
